data.title: A look at pricey high-flying stocks in the industrial sector
data.description:
Wall Street investors are increasingly seeking refuge in high-performing equity plays as volatile industrial markets continue to shift, forcing a critical evaluation of stock price velocity against fundamental underlying valuations.

Analysts warn that chasing recent momentum can leave market participants overexposed to highly priced assets, prompting a rush toward selective screens that highlight cheap high flyers within the aerospace, defense, machinery, and electrical equipment sectors.

Below is a list of the top 10 industrials sector stocks, spanning aerospace, defense, machinery, and electrical equipment, with top momentum grades paired with weaker valuation metrics across various market capitalizations.

The list is led by ATI Inc. (ATI), with a momentum grade of A+ and valuation grade of C-. Astronics Corporation (ATRO) and Bloom Energy Corporation (BE) follow, both earning perfect A+ momentum ratings. Carpenter Technology Corporation (CRS) and Ducommun Incorporated (DCO) round out the top five. Other high momentum performers include First Advantage Corporation (FA), IES Holdings, Inc. (IESC), and Moog Inc. (MOG.A), with Paycom Software, Inc. (PAYC) and Preformed Line Products Company (PLPC) completing the top ten.

Momentum grades reflect price velocity and performance on a scale from A+ (strongest upward trend) to F. Valuation grades measure how cheap or expensive a stock is relative to fundamentals, with A+ indicating the most undervalued and F representing the most overvalued.

data.title: Magazine Luiza S.A. reports Q2 results
Verastem outlines October VS-7375 response-rate update while targeting LGSOC self-sustainability by end of 2026
data.description:
Earnings Call Insights: Verastem Oncology (VSTM) Q2 2026

Management View

  • CEO Daniel Paterson said the quarter delivered both commercial and pipeline momentum: "We delivered a strong second quarter with meaningful progress across both our commercial business and pipeline" and reported "net product revenues of $25.1 million," which he said reflected execution that is "putting us back on track and reinforcing the long-term opportunity for AVMAPKI FAKZYNJA CO-PACK."
  • Paterson highlighted balance-sheet actions and timing: "We also strengthened the balance sheet with a non-dilutive royalty financing agreement with Oberland Capital to secure up to $75 million in funding, of which we expect to draw $50 million at closing," and added that "a $15 million milestone payment from Secura Bio" together represented "the incremental $90 million in non-dilutive funding" that "strengthens our balance sheet" and "preserves strategic flexibility."
  • On the LGSOC launch trajectory, Paterson said, "we continue to expect the LGSOC business will become self-sustaining by the end of 2026," and described a Q1-to-Q2 rebound: "Since the first quarter, we've seen a meaningful rebound with significant quarter-over-quarter growth" driven by "growing physician confidence," earlier-line use, and "increasing patient refills."
  • Chief Commercial Officer Daniel Lyons said the launch focus remains: "driving consistent new patient demand, expanding use earlier in the treatment journey, and helping patients to stay on therapy," and added, "we drove meaningful growth in the adoption of the CO-PACK, and we are seeing that momentum continue in Q3."
  • CFO Daniel Calkins said spending discipline remains intact: "we expect SG&A expenses to remain roughly the same on a quarterly basis throughout 2026," and stated, "we believe we have sufficient capital to fund operations into the second half of 2027."

Outlook

  • Paterson laid out second-half priorities: "Drive strong execution of our commercial strategy to expand adoption of AVMAPKI FAKZYNJA CO-PACK, complete enrollment in our three Phase II registration-directed VS-7375 trials, and prepare to initiate our three Phase III trials for VS-7375."
  • On the next clinical catalyst, Paterson said, "In October, we expect to provide a more comprehensive data set for VS-7375, including response rates across our three lead tumor types, pancreatic, lung, and colorectal cancers, with approximately 20 patients in each, as well as an early look at durability."
  • In Q&A, President of Development Michael Glen Kauffman reinforced the accelerated-approval framing: "30% is a great metric in this disease. Six months is also terrific," adding that regulators consider "both activity as well as the safety and tolerability profile."

Financial Results

  • Calkins reported $25.1 million in net product revenue, $3.8 million in product cost of sales, and "$15 million in license revenue" tied to COPIKTRA, which he said was triggered when "cumulative worldwide net sales of COPIKTRA surpassing $200 million during the second quarter of 2026."
  • Calkins reported operating expenses of $41.3 million in R&D and $27.4 million in SG&A, and said non-GAAP adjusted net loss was $30.6 million, or $0.31 per diluted share.
  • On liquidity, Calkins said cash, equivalents, and investments were $136.4 million at quarter-end; he added, "our pro forma cash balance at the end of the second quarter is $201.4 million" when including the Oberland closing draw and the COPIKTRA milestone.

Q&A

  • Eric Schmidt, Cantor Fitzgerald: asked about G12D partnership activity; CEO Paterson said, "We continue to work on the Erasca partnership" and cited "considerable inbound interest from strategics," adding the new financing "gives us a lot more strategic flexibility to not have to rush." CFO Calkins, on margins, said, "Yes, I think that is a reasonable run" given cost of sales is "still continues to be royalty-based."
  • Michelle Boisvert, Guggenheim: asked whether "30% overall response rate and six months durability" remains the right bar; President Kauffman said, "We think that's generally a very good guidepost" and emphasized tolerability tradeoffs versus rash/stomatitis.
  • Joshua Wolfson, RBC: asked about translating GenFleet China ORR to the U.S.; CEO Paterson said, "the most important benchmarks are going to be the U.S. data" and President Kauffman added, "Direct translation, probably not direct, but within the ballpark."
  • Faisal Khurshid, Jefferies: asked whether CO-PACK growth was new starts vs. duration; CCO Lyons said, "It's a bit of both," citing "meaningful increase in new prescribers and new accounts" plus encouraging refill execution.
  • Graig Suvannavejh, Mizuho: asked what will drive sales and how VS-7375 differentiates; CCO Lyons said, "you need all three" (new starts, earlier line, persistence), while CEO Paterson said versus panRAS they intend "better efficacy and significantly better tolerability," and President Kauffman said, "We have no rash and no mucositis" and PK "continues to climb" from 400 to 600 to 900.
  • Andres Maldonado, H.C. Wainwright: asked about earlier-line prescribing and CRC strategy; CEO Paterson said, "we don't intend to develop it as a single agent. It's going to be with an EGFR inhibitor," and CCO Lyons said earlier-line movement is occurring "not only in the academic, but also in the community" with dose interruptions expected but managed.
  • Jeet Mukherjee, BTIG: asked PRMT5 strategy and FDA bar; CEO Paterson said, "we're exploring all options," while President Kauffman said, "The FDA has never told us what they need" but called "30% ORR with at least six months durability" a "great rule of thumb."
  • Matthew Venezia, Alliance Global Partners: asked how physicians choose between panRAS and trials; President Kauffman said the discussion is "an efficacy and a tolerability discussion" and added, "they would recommend for a G12D patient that they go on to a G12D specific drug" given tolerability concerns with panRAS.

Sentiment Analysis

  • Analysts’ tone was slightly positive, repeatedly referencing a "strong quarter" and probing durability/competitiveness (e.g., Guggenheim asked if the "competitive landscape in PDAC" changes what’s needed).
  • Management’s tone was positive and confident in prepared remarks (Paterson: "strong second quarter"), while remaining measured in Q&A on partnering timing (Paterson: "it's really a judgment call on how early or late you do a partnership") and relying on rule-of-thumb approval thresholds (Kauffman: "The FDA has never told us what they need").
  • Versus last quarter, Q2 messaging shifted from explaining "seasonal headwinds" and launch fixes to emphasizing a rebound (Paterson: "meaningful rebound") and incremental non-dilutive capital that reduces near-term financing pressure.

Quarter-over-quarter Comparison

  • The biggest change in emphasis was commercial momentum: Q1 discussed insurance/weather headwinds and later-line discontinuations; Q2 stressed that "the changes we made are having an impact" and highlighted increased refills and earlier-line use.
  • Capital strategy shifted from intent to find nondilutive options in Q1 to announcing a specific facility in Q2: "up to $75 million" with an expected "$50 million" draw at closing, plus the $15 million milestone.
  • The VS-7375 narrative moved from describing Phase II initiations and dose work in Q1 to setting a defined data event in Q2: "response rates" across three tumor types expected in October.

Risks and Concerns

  • Management cited launch execution risks tied to real-world persistence and line of therapy, emphasizing mitigation through field support to "help patients stay on therapy" and active adverse-event management.
  • On VS-7375 differentiation risk in a crowded landscape, CEO Paterson framed competitive priorities as "better efficacy and significantly better tolerability," while President Kauffman highlighted class-related tolerability concerns (rash, mucositis/stomatitis) and stated, "We have no rash and no mucositis."
  • On partnering/financing uncertainty, Paterson pointed to timing tradeoffs and said the new funding provides flexibility to "not have to rush into something nor rush into an equity financing."

Final Takeaway

Management framed Q2 as a commercial re-acceleration for AVMAPKI FAKZYNJA CO-PACK alongside a clearer catalyst path for VS-7375, anchored by an October update with response rates across pancreatic, lung, and colorectal cohorts. Leadership also emphasized added financial flexibility via the Oberland royalty financing and the COPIKTRA milestone, while reiterating the goal for the LGSOC franchise to be self-sustaining by the end of 2026 and for current capital to fund operations into the second half of 2027.

data.title: Weave anticipates $273M-$275M 2026 revenue while raising operating income outlook to $12M-$14M
data.description:
Earnings Call Insights: Weave Communications (WEAV) Q2 2026

Management View

  • Brett White (CEO & Director) said, "We've delivered strong results in the second quarter." He reported "Total revenue was $67.5 million, 15.5% growth over last year," and added that "Revenue retention measured on a quarterly basis also improved sequentially" and the company "added the most new locations ever in a single quarter, both on a gross and net basis."

  • White highlighted vertical performance, saying, "Dental, our largest vertical, had a strong quarter," and described specialty medical progress: "we released a significantly deeper integration with the athenaOne platform and joined athenahealth's Marketplace, making our innovative solutions available to more than 160,000 specialty medical providers."

  • On profitability and go-to-market efficiency, White said, "sales and marketing expense as a percentage of revenue was down sequentially" and "we expanded our operating margin to almost 5%, up sharply from roughly breakeven in the same quarter last year." He also flagged execution friction during a sales transition: "it took time to calibrate the lead distribution with the appropriate execution, resulting in bookings slightly below our expectation despite very strong demand."

  • Jason Christiansen (Chief Financial Officer) said, "The second quarter of 2026 was a solid quarter for Weave with continued revenue growth and much improved operating income," and noted a "slight headwind to Q2 revenue was a quarter-over-quarter and year-over-year decrease in onboarding revenue due to lower setup fees," adding, "Moving forward, we are renewing our focus on consistently collecting these onetime setup fees."

Outlook

  • Christiansen guided full-year 2026 revenue to "the range of $273 million to $275 million," saying it "reflects the impact of the go-to-market transition adjustment period" described by White.

  • Christiansen raised profitability expectations, saying, "we are raising our non-GAAP operating income guidance" and now expects "$12 million to $14 million," tying the change to "improvements in operating efficiency" from go-to-market initiatives.

  • For Q3 2026, Christiansen projected revenue of "$68.6 million to $69.6 million" and operating income of "$3 million to $4 million," and provided expected share count of "approximately 80.2 million shares" for Q3.

  • Compared with Q1 2026, the company’s full-year revenue outlook moved from "$275 million to $278 million" to "$273 million to $275 million," while full-year non-GAAP operating income outlook moved from "$10.5 million to $13.5 million" to "$12 million to $14 million."

Financial Results

  • Christiansen reported gross profit of "$49 million" and gross margin of "72.6%," and said sequential gross margin pressure reflected "increased usage fees for messaging and true-up invoices on certain vendor agreements" plus "an increase in credit card fees" tied to annual prepay cohorts.

  • Christiansen reported retention of "GRR was 89% and NRR was 92%," and emphasized that reported retention is "a weighted average of the previous 12 months monthly retention rates" and "it can take multiple quarters for improvements to show through in reported metrics."

  • Christiansen reported operating income of "$3.2 million" and said it "exceeded the top end of our guidance," adding that sales and marketing efficiency was a key driver as sales and marketing expense was "$25.8 million or 38% of revenue."

  • On cash generation, Christiansen said Weave ended with "$78.5 million in cash and short-term investments," with "cash from operating activities in Q2" of "$10.2 million" and "free cash flow" of "$8.7 million," adding, "We were free cash flow positive for the first half of 2026."

Q&A

  • Alex Sklar, Raymond James: asked how "record gross in net locations" and payments growth reconcile with a "lower growth outlook"; Jason Christiansen (CFO): said the impact stems from the May-to-July sales transition where "demand remained very strong" but lead distribution issues will "flow through in the back half of the year"; Brett White (CEO): added, "bookings shortfalls in May, June and July" will show up in "Q3" and "into Q4."

  • Alex Sklar, Raymond James: asked about May-to-July linearity, Q4 improvement assumptions, and sales team sizing; Brett White (CEO): said inbound verticalization is already showing "positive results," while outbound "got disrupted May to July" and the company "completed the transition first week in August"; on headcount, he stated, "the team size is smaller" and some sellers moved into SDR roles.

  • Alex Sklar, Raymond James: asked about specialty medical opportunity from athenahealth integration and upsell; Brett White (CEO): said, "Getting a deeper integration into athenahealth is huge" and described moving from "1 to 4" on integration levels; Jason Christiansen (CFO): explained Level 4 brings "read and write capabilities across multiple tables" and said integrated areas are already showing improved ASPs.

  • Hannah Rudoff, Piper Sandler: asked how long go-to-market disruption could persist and confidence in the guide; Jason Christiansen (CFO): said guidance reflects "our best thinking" and the accelerated cutover should have the business "back to executing" within "the next couple of months."

  • Hannah Rudoff, Piper Sandler: asked if demand weakened via sales cycles or budget scrutiny; Brett White (CEO): said, "I haven't seen any slacking a slackening of the demand environment" and added the disruption "was not demand related at all," also noting, "we announced a partnership with the American Dental Association... and it's doing really well."

  • J. Lane, Stifel: asked what drove stronger dental net adds and sustainability; Brett White (CEO): attributed it to focus from verticalizing inbound sales and marketing; Jason Christiansen (CFO): cited ADA partnership and said the company views the period as "a ripple in the path."

  • Mark Schappel, Loop Capital Markets: asked how AI engagement translates into financial results (ARPU/retention/revenue); Brett White (CEO): said AI modules are monetized "additionally and/or... part of an upsell" and also make Weave "stickier" and "easier to sell"; Jason Christiansen (CFO): differentiated AI features that are not explicitly monetized versus "net new incremental capabilities like AI receptionist"; White added that AI-driven workflows can expand "payments volume" and said, "we've got accelerating payments volume growth."

Sentiment Analysis

  • Analyst tone was slightly negative to neutral, focusing on guide reset durability and execution risk around sales model changes, with repeated probing on the "lower growth outlook" and how long disruption could persist.

  • Management tone was slightly positive in prepared remarks and more explanatory in Q&A, repeatedly characterizing the issue as execution rather than demand; White said, "I haven't seen any slacking a slackening of the demand environment," while Christiansen emphasized the guide reflects "our best thinking" after accelerating the transition.

  • Versus Q1 2026, management language shifted from emphasizing repeated guidance outperformance (Q1: "Both revenue and profitability came in above the high end of our guidance") to emphasizing a transition-related adjustment (Q2: "resulting in bookings slightly below our expectation") alongside a higher operating income outlook.

Quarter-over-Quarter Comparison

  • The biggest change was guidance direction: Q1 raised full-year revenue to "$275 million to $278 million," while Q2 reduced it to "$273 million to $275 million" and explicitly tied the change to the "go-to-market transition adjustment period" and "bookings shortfalls" during May to July.

  • Profit focus intensified: Q2 highlighted a sequential decline in sales and marketing expense as a percentage of revenue and raised full-year operating income guidance to "$12 million to $14 million," compared with "$10.5 million to $13.5 million" in Q1.

  • Strategic emphasis moved from product rollout timing in Q1 (omnichannel AI Receptionist broader availability discussed) to execution and organizational design in Q2, including inbound verticalization and completing the outbound SDR transition in early August.

  • Analyst questioning in Q1 centered more on AI Receptionist pricing and NRR mechanics, while Q2 concentrated on the revenue outlook reset and the operational impact of go-to-market changes.

Risks and Concerns

  • Christiansen identified onboarding revenue pressure from "lower setup fees" and said Weave is "renewing our focus" on collecting setup fees going forward.

  • Christiansen cited gross margin pressures from "increased usage fees for messaging" and "true-up invoices on certain vendor agreements," plus higher credit card fees from annual prepay cohorts.

  • White described execution risk in the sales transition, saying lead calibration issues caused "bookings slightly below our expectation" and that the impact is reflected in the revenue outlook.

  • White also highlighted unrealized value in AI-driven opportunities, noting call intelligence surfaced "810,000 unscheduled opportunities" and said "Only a portion of these opportunities were acted upon by staff," framing AI receptionist as a tool to close that gap.

Final Takeaway

Management described Q2 as a quarter of record location additions, expanding operating profitability, and accelerating AI engagement, while also acknowledging that a May-to-July outbound sales transition created a bookings shortfall that is now embedded in a lowered full-year revenue range. The company paired that revenue reset with higher full-year operating income guidance, attributing the profitability lift to sales and marketing efficiency gains and a faster completion of the SDR-led outbound model in early August, alongside continued investment in deeper vertical integrations such as athenahealth and monetized AI modules like AI Receptionist and Call Intelligence.

data.title: B2Gold granted Fekola Regional exploitation permit by Mali government
data.description:
B2Gold (BTG) up 22.2% in Friday's trading after saying the Mali government granted the Menankoto exploitation permit, which, together with the Dandoko exploration permit, comprises Fekola Regional, a key near-term production growth driver for the company.

The issuance of the Menankoto exploitation permit follows a year of talks that culminated in the receipt of both the approval to commence underground mining operations at the Fekola Mine in July 2025 and now the issuance of the Menankoto exploitation permit.

The Fekola complex is the largest producing gold mine in Mali, and the issuance of the Menankoto exploitation permit secures the future of the operation well into the late 2030s, the company said.

Fekola Regional is expected to ramp up operations through the end of 2027, and produce at least 150K oz/year from 2028 through the mid-2030's.

Shares of precious metals showed strong gains across the board Friday as gold prices surged following the July non-farm payrolls report that showed a contraction of 23K jobs, a weaker-than-expected showing that may reduce the likelihood for interest rate hikes by the U.S. Federal Reserve.

data.title: Pain drug developer Latigo climbs after upsized IPO
data.description:
Latigo Biotherapeutics (LTGO), a clinical-stage biopharma focused on developing non-opioid pain medicines, rose sharply on its first day of trading after an upsized initial public offering that raised over $300M.

Shares opened for trading at $21 apiece around 11:40 am ET from the IPO price of $18.00 per share, indicating a roughly 17% gain and a market capitalization of over $1.3B for the Thousand Oaks, California-based company.

Late Thursday, Latigo (LTGO) priced the offering of 19.2M shares at the top of the marketed range, projecting $345.6M in gross proceeds excluding the underwriters’ 30-day option for roughly 2.9M additional shares.

Earlier this month, the Blue Owl Capital (OBDC)-backed firm updated its IPO plans, indicating it would offer 16M shares at $16 - $18 each to raise about $247.2M. The company intends to use its net proceeds, among other purposes, to further advance its lead asset, LTG-001, in late-stage development toward filing a marketing application with the FDA.

As for upcoming catalysts, in H2 2026, Latigo (LTGO) plans to begin two Phase 3 trials to test LTG-001 in patients undergoing bunionectomy and a broader group of patients with moderate to severe acute pain. Topline results from those placebo-controlled and open-label studies are expected in H2 2027.

data.title: Clean energy fuels keeps $70M-$75M adjusted EBITDA outlook as 45Z could add up to $5M
data.description:
Earnings Call Insights: Clean Energy Fuels (CLNE) Q2 2026

Management View

  • "Today, we reported solid results for the second quarter, $106 million of revenue, $63 million of RNG sold and $16 million of adjusted EBITDA." (President, CEO & Director Barclay Corbus)
  • "These results were in line with our expectations and keep us on track for our annual financial outlook, which we are maintaining." (President, CEO & Director Corbus)
  • "Our upstream RNG production business saw improvement in the second quarter, helped by better weather compared to the first quarter and continued ramp-up at our 2 largest projects, South Fork in Texas and East Valley in Idaho." (President, CEO & Director Corbus)
  • "We continue to await Treasury's finalization of the 45Z rules and credit values, which is now expected in the fourth quarter." (President, CEO & Director Corbus)
  • "Last week, we announced the latest and largest hydrogen project to date, a $27 million contract with Orange County Transportation Authority to design and build a new private station." (President, CEO & Director Corbus)
  • "Finally, I want to recognize Bart Frabotta, who we recently appointed as our Chief Operating Officer." (President, CEO & Director Corbus)
  • "Overall, our second quarter performance was in line with our expectations from both the financial performance and fuel volume standpoint." (Chief Financial Officer Robert Vreeland)

Outlook

  • "Maintaining our full year guidance assumes improved financial performance in the second half of 2026, which is consistent with our original expectations." (Chief Financial Officer Vreeland)
  • "Our outlook for 2026 also assumes that final guidance on the GREET model for the 45Z production tax credit will be issued before year-end, and that could provide up to $5 million of incremental adjusted EBITDA." (Chief Financial Officer Vreeland)
  • "Now if the guidance is delayed or provides minimal benefit over the current production tax credit values, adjusted EBITDA would come in below our $70 million to $75 million range." (Chief Financial Officer Vreeland)
  • Compared with Q1, management updated its timing expectation for 45Z, stating the finalization is "now expected in the fourth quarter" (President, CEO & Director Corbus) and emphasizing timing risk to 2026 results (Chief Financial Officer Vreeland).

Financial Results

  • "Second quarter fuel volumes increased by 7% year-over-year to 81.8 million gallons." (Chief Financial Officer Vreeland)
  • "RNG volumes increased 3% year-over-year to 63.2 million gallons, reflecting normal variations across customer sectors." (Chief Financial Officer Vreeland)
  • "RNG production volume from our dairy projects was 2.1 million gallons for the second quarter of 2026, well above the prior year period as our RNG upstream portfolio continues to ramp." (Chief Financial Officer Vreeland)
  • "Second quarter revenue was $106.4 million -- up from $106.4 million, up from $102.6 million in the prior year period." (Chief Financial Officer Vreeland)
  • "Our cash and investments of $138 million at the end of June were up from $126 million at the end of March." (Chief Financial Officer Vreeland)

Q&A

  • Eric Stine, Craig-Hallum Capital Group LLC, Research Division: "could you maybe talk about what you're seeing in terms of the incremental cost" for the X15N? President, CEO & Director Corbus: "I don't think we've seen real movement in the sort of actual price" and added, "we poured a lot more money into advertising to highlight that... which impacted our results, but we think it was an absolutely good investment in the long term."
  • Eric Stine, Craig-Hallum Capital Group LLC, Research Division: asked whether 45Z was upside to guidance; Chief Financial Officer Vreeland: "we factored up to about $5 million in our guidance" and said the key variable is timing, adding, "if they moved the -- whatever approval across into '27... it wouldn't happen for us in '26."
  • Rob Brown, Lake Street Capital Markets, LLC, Research Division: asked how diesel prices are affecting adoption; President, CEO & Director Corbus: "when you have all this uncertainty that's going on with the regulatory environment" fleets "wait to see how things settle out here before we make a big commitment."
  • Rob Brown, Lake Street Capital Markets, LLC, Research Division: asked about upstream RNG profitability trajectory; President, CEO & Director Corbus: "It will be the second half of the year will be much better than the first half of the year" and added, "we are optimistic."
  • Nathaniel Pendleton, Texas Capital Securities, Research Division: asked about off-grid/power generation opportunity size and investment; President, CEO & Director Corbus: "in order to test this market, we don't have to spend anything" and described using "existing assets and existing infrastructure we have."
  • Nathaniel Pendleton, Texas Capital Securities, Research Division: asked about hydrogen opportunity cadence; President, CEO & Director Corbus: "The way that we've gone about hydrogen is not to use our own capital" and described winning transit RFPs on a "cost-plus contract" model.
  • Matthew Lovseth Blair, Tudor, Pickering, Holt & Co., LLC: asked LCFS pathway timing; President, CEO & Director Corbus: "it's entirely dependent on CARB" and said, "we'd hope the end of 2027 and 2028, but we're not putting anything in our forecast to move from temporary to provisional." Chief Financial Officer Vreeland added, "We're monetizing at the temporary level."

Sentiment Analysis

  • Analysts: slightly negative to pressing, repeatedly probing adoption friction and policy timing, including "slower on the uptake" (Eric Stine, Craig-Hallum Capital Group LLC, Research Division) and CARB timing concerns around "a reasonable timeline" (Matthew Lovseth Blair, Tudor, Pickering, Holt & Co., LLC).
  • Management: slightly positive in prepared remarks and more explanatory in Q&A, highlighting optionality but acknowledging uncertainty, including "there is still more work to be done" (President, CEO & Director Corbus) and framing 45Z as timing-sensitive: "it's more about timing" (Chief Financial Officer Vreeland).
  • Versus Q1, the tone shifted from introducing a new CEO and emphasizing diesel volatility to more operational execution themes, including upstream ramp progress and "Improving execution and operational performance" tied to the COO appointment (President, CEO & Director Corbus).

Quarter-over-Quarter Comparison

  • Q2 introduced additional growth vectors beyond vehicle fuel, with President, CEO & Director Corbus saying "we see emerging opportunities for clean energy and our ability to serve independent power solutions" and citing new CNG-to-power contracting; Q1 focused more heavily on trucking adoption and RNG fundamentals.
  • Q2 highlighted a new senior leadership move: "we recently appointed as our Chief Operating Officer" (President, CEO & Director Corbus); Q1 centered on Corbus’s CEO transition and Andrew Littlefair’s ongoing board/policy role.
  • On policy, Q2 pushed expected 45Z timing to "the fourth quarter" (President, CEO & Director Corbus), while Q1 described awaiting an upgraded GREET model without specifying Q4.
  • Analysts’ focus remained consistent on X15N adoption and regulatory drivers, while adding deeper questioning on LCFS pathway timing and LCFS market dynamics in Q2.

Risks and Concerns

  • "with the uncertainty surrounding the final 2027 emission standards recently released by the EPA, there has been a large prebuy of legacy diesel trucks" (President, CEO & Director Corbus), which management linked to slower near-term NG truck conversion.
  • "We continue to await Treasury's finalization of the 45Z rules" (President, CEO & Director Corbus) and "if the guidance is delayed" adjusted EBITDA could fall "below our $70 million to $75 million range" (Chief Financial Officer Vreeland).
  • "it's entirely dependent on CARB" for LCFS pathway timing, and management stated, "we're not putting anything in our forecast to move from temporary to provisional" (President, CEO & Director Corbus).

Final Takeaway

Management characterized Q2 results as tracking plan while keeping the full-year adjusted EBITDA outlook at $70 million to $75 million, with a key swing factor being the timing and value of 45Z guidance that could contribute up to $5 million. Leadership emphasized improving upstream RNG execution into the second half, continued cautious progress on heavy-duty trucking adoption amid regulatory uncertainty, and highlighted non-capital-intensive expansion opportunities in off-grid natural gas solutions and cost-plus hydrogen station buildouts, including a $27 million OCTA contract.

data.title: Under Armour forecasts mid-single-digit revenue decline while maintaining $140M-$160M adjusted operating income outlook
data.description:
Earnings Call Insights: Under Armour (UAA) Q1 fiscal 2027

Management View

  • "We're lowering our revenue outlook for the year while maintaining our adjusted operating income expectation." (CEO Kevin Plank)
  • "Consumer demand remains softer than we expected, particularly in North America and Asia Pacific." (CEO Plank)
  • "We're testing more full-price product in this environment." (CEO Plank)
  • "Building on the 25% reduction we've already achieved in our fall/winter '26 assortment compared to just 2 years ago, we've begun targeting a further 25% SKU reduction over the next 18 months." (CEO Plank)
  • "Launched in May, Bouncy has exceeded expectations while selling at its full $65 retail price." (CEO Plank)
  • "Given this amplified focus, we're taking marketing lower as a percentage of revenue this year." (CEO Plank)
  • "Revenue declined 3% to $1.1 billion." (CFO Reza Taleghani)
  • "Gross margin increased 590 basis points year-over-year to 54.1% in the first quarter." (CFO Taleghani)
  • "Adjusted operating income was $52 million, exceeding our outlook of $30 million to $40 million." (CFO Taleghani)

Outlook

  • "We now expect this year's revenue to decline at a mid-single-digit rate, but we are maintaining our adjusted operating income outlook of $140 million to $160 million." (CFO Taleghani)
  • "We continue to expect expansion of approximately 220 to 270 basis points versus last year" on gross margin, including "roughly 150 basis points of benefit" from IEEPA tariff refunds. (CFO Taleghani)
  • "We've also updated our outlook for adjusted SG&A, which we now expect to decline at a low single-digit rate versus last year." (CFO Taleghani)
  • "For the second quarter, we expect revenue to decline at a high single-digit rate" and "second quarter adjusted operating income of $10 million to $20 million and an adjusted diluted loss per share of $0.01 to $0.03." (CFO Taleghani)

Financial Results

  • "Revenue declined 3% to $1.1 billion" with "North America revenue decreased 9%," "EMEA revenue increased 12%," and "revenue in APAC decreased 7%." (CFO Taleghani)
  • "Direct-to-consumer revenue decreased 6% in the quarter" including "a 12% decline in e-com." (CFO Taleghani)
  • "Footwear revenue was down 8%" and "our run business was flat in the quarter." (CFO Taleghani)
  • "First quarter diluted earnings per share was breakeven" and "our adjusted diluted earnings per share for the quarter was $0.05." (CFO Taleghani)
  • "We ended the quarter with $1.1 billion in inventory, down 3% year-over-year" and "$396 million in cash." (CFO Taleghani)
  • "We completed an amendment to our revolving credit facility earlier this week" and "the amendment is leverage neutral and not related to near-term funding need." (CFO Taleghani)

Q&A

  • Jay Sole, UBS: asked about the Bouncy Tee’s intentionality and repeatability; CEO Plank: "we wanted something that could really demonstrate the full price nature of Under Armour" and "this becomes the metaphor of the plan" for future launches.
  • Jay Sole, UBS: asked how UA can cut sales guidance but keep discipline on margins/inventory; CEO Plank: "we can increase the efficacy" of spend and "we are finding leverage in the business."
  • Sam Poser, Williams Trading: pressed on what “sportswear” means and how big it is; CEO Plank: sportswear is "a product that were intended to be worn with all the performance attributes of UA" in non-sport settings, and Bouncy Tee "walks the line."
  • Sam Poser, Williams Trading: challenged SKU reduction and implications for inventory/promotions; CEO Plank: "there is going to be some near-term trade-off" and CFO Taleghani: "you can do that in the natural sales cycle."
  • Robert Drbul, BTIG: asked what changed over 90 days on revenue and what marketing is focused on; CEO Plank: traffic "precipitously got weaker" from "mid- to late May" and marketing needs to be "more coordinated" to convert sports moments into sales.
  • Brooke Roach, Goldman Sachs: asked if North America pullback is strategic vs. macro and about wholesale cancellations; CFO Taleghani: Q2 reflects macro trends, back half improvement is tied to "product launches" and "continued marketplace discipline."
  • John Elias, on for Guggenheim: asked what offsets lower revenue to hold operating income; CFO Taleghani: "we are basically saying that we're going to do better" on SG&A and "we overdelivered on Q1."
  • Brian Nagel, Oppenheimer: asked whether weakness is across products and about marketing spend; CEO Plank: "we do have great product right now" but must improve storytelling, and CFO Taleghani: marketing will be "at the lower end" of the 10% to 11% range, implying "a reduction in absolute dollars."
  • Peter McGoldrick, Stifel: asked about capital structure and IEEPA refunds; CFO Taleghani: "the IEEPA refunds have come in" and UA expects "free cash flow positive this year" and "There's no M&A on the horizon."

Sentiment Analysis

  • Slightly negative: analysts repeatedly pressed on the revenue guide cut, North America/China demand, promotional intensity, and the mechanics of maintaining profit with lower sales (e.g., Brooke Roach asking how much is macro vs. proactive, and Sam Poser challenging whether inventory should fall faster than sales).
  • Neutral to slightly positive: management emphasized discipline and avoided promising a near-term demand inflection, repeatedly stating "We're not going to chase the market down" (CEO Plank) while defending profit protection through cost control and marketing efficiency.
  • Compared with last quarter, management language shifted from expecting marketing investment to "move higher" to "taking marketing lower as a percentage of revenue" (CEO Plank), while analysts’ questioning in the current call focused more on demand deterioration since late May and promotion pressure.

Quarter-over-Quarter Comparison

  • Current call: "lowering our revenue outlook for the year" (CEO Plank) versus the prior call’s full-year framing that revenue would be "down slightly" (CFO Taleghani, prior transcript).
  • Marketing stance changed from prior guidance of "additional marketing investments" and staying within "10% to 12% of revenue" (CFO Taleghani, prior transcript) to now expecting marketing at a lower percentage of revenue and the "lower end" of 10% to 11% (CEO Plank; CFO Taleghani).
  • Current Q&A centered on a more promotional environment and traffic softness starting "mid- to late May" (CEO Plank); prior quarter Q&A leaned more toward defining “stabilization,” gross margin drivers, and e-commerce reset plans.

Risks and Concerns

  • "Traffic softened" and the marketplace became "increasingly promotional" in North America and Asia Pacific. (CEO Plank)
  • China challenges included "stock-outs" and "demand cannibalization from certain licensees that discounted aggressively"; management said it is being addressed through "better inventory availability and closer alignment with licensing partners." (CFO Taleghani)
  • Supply chain risk was flagged as "pressure related to the Middle East conflict" and tariff uncertainty, with management reiterating a "10% tariff assumption" through fiscal year-end. (CFO Taleghani)

Final Takeaway

Management said it is resetting Under Armour toward fewer, higher-impact products and more disciplined marketplace execution, cutting the full-year revenue outlook to a mid-single-digit decline while holding adjusted operating income guidance at $140 million to $160 million. Executives emphasized full-price demand creation (highlighting the $65 Bouncy Tee), targeted additional SKU reductions over the next 18 months, tighter SG&A control, and a shift to more efficient marketing spend, while citing softer traffic trends since late May and heightened promotional pressure—especially in North America, parts of Asia Pacific, and the U.K./Europe.

data.title: Ready Capital outlines $1.5B SBA 7(a) origination target as it reaches 81% of liquidity objective
data.description:
Earnings Call Insights: Ready Capital Corporation (RC) Q2 2026

Management View

  • "The second quarter of 2026 demonstrates meaningful progress in our balance sheet repositioning strategy" (Chairman, CEO & Chief Investment Officer Thomas Capasse), adding, "we do not anticipate further large portfolio sales" and "we have been organizing our work this year around 4 priorities" including "strengthening liquidity," "resolving non and subperforming CRE assets," "transitioning to a lower-cost business model," and "focusing on growth in our small business SBA 7(a) lending."
  • "Since our first quarter earnings" the company completed actions including "the sale of our $167 million construction portfolio," "the securitization of $158 million of unguaranteed SBA 7(a) loans at a 92% advance priced at SOFR plus 240 basis points," "the disposition of $445 million of CRE assets," and "the successful refinance of the Portland Ritz asset into a CPACE loan" (Chairman, CEO & Chief Investment Officer Capasse). He said these actions "have generated approximately $1.9 billion of cash" and "we now have achieved approximately 81% of our target liquidity objective."
  • "The current earnings drag across our non and subperforming and REO was $0.29 per share in the quarter" (Chairman, CEO & Chief Investment Officer Capasse). On SBA 7(a), he said Q2 originations were constrained, but "we expect steady growth towards our annual target of $1.5 billion of originations" and "we intend to accelerate our capital levels through more frequent SBA 7(a) ABS offerings."
  • "For the quarter, we reported a GAAP loss from continuing operations of $0.63 per common share" (CFO & Secretary Andrew Ahlborn). He added, "distributable earnings were a loss of $0.47 per common share" and "book value per share was $6.83 versus $7.43 at March 31."

Outlook

  • Management did not provide explicit EPS or revenue guidance in the prepared remarks or Q&A.
  • "We are no longer budgeting loan sales at this stage" (Chairman, CEO & Chief Investment Officer Capasse), framing remaining liquidity drivers as "the optimization of financing on $950 million of performing and nonperforming loans and runoff on $900 million, and a potential sale or financing on a $118 million joint venture position," which he said "will generate liquidity in excess of the 2026 remaining maturities."
  • "Those 3 things will result in a targeted 25% to 35% reduction in OpEx" (Chairman, CEO & Chief Investment Officer Capasse), tied to "divestiture of ancillary businesses" and "integration with the external manager's CRE lending businesses to source investments."

Financial Results

  • "Recurring revenue was $15.3 million compared to $16.2 million in the prior quarter" (CFO & Secretary Ahlborn). He attributed the shift to "an $8.7 million improvement in the net interest loss" offset by "a $2 million reduction in gain on sale revenue" and "a $7.5 million reduction in other recurring revenue."
  • "Operating expenses improved to $48.7 million from $67.7 million" (CFO & Secretary Ahlborn), primarily from "normalization of servicing expenses to $3.4 million from $15.4 million" after Q1 items related to "nonrecurring servicer advance reimbursements tied to the first quarter CLO collapses."
  • "We ended the quarter with $124.1 million of unrestricted cash" (CFO & Secretary Ahlborn). He also said "total assets declined to $6.26 billion" and "total leverage was 3x, trending towards our 2.5x target," with "$690 million of unencumbered assets."

Q&A

  • Crispin Love, Piper Sandler & Co.: "on meeting the fourth quarter debt maturities, can you share just what else needs to be done" and "what are you targeting for the remainder of 2026 as it relates for CRE and ... dispositions and runoff?" Chairman, CEO & Chief Investment Officer Capasse replied, "we're in the ... eighth inning" and said the plan centers on "optimization" of financing on "$950 million" of loans, "runoff on $900 million," and action on the "$118 million joint venture position," with loan sales only "opportunistically."
  • Crispin Love, Piper Sandler & Co.: asked about "potential monetization" of the Portland mixed-use property; Chairman, CEO & Chief Investment Officer Capasse said "that will lead to a decision to monetize it at some point in the next ... coming quarters," describing "linear improvement" at the hotel and progress on condo sell-through.
  • Jade Rahmani, KBW: asked, "Can you say more about the $118 million joint venture investment?" Chairman, CEO & Chief Investment Officer Capasse said it is "essentially an LP interest in a Waterfall-managed CRE fund" and later added it is "a straight-up LP interest in a fund that's in its harvest period" and that the company is evaluating "fund financing on LP interest as well as a secondary market for sale."
  • Jade Rahmani, KBW: questioned leverage on the CRE book and the feasibility of avoiding asset sales; CFO & Secretary Ahlborn said asset-level "average advance rates ... are in the low 60s" and described corporate secured debt as "equity pledges of entities throughout the structure." Chairman, CEO & Chief Investment Officer Capasse responded, "we constantly evaluate ... the discount for sale in the secondary market versus on-balance sheet strategies" and said there is "a lot of liquidity available for these assets."
  • Jade Rahmani, KBW: asked whether the company can return to profitability; Chairman, CEO & Chief Investment Officer Capasse answered, "Yes," outlining "the runoff of the legacy book," ramping SBA (which he called "highly profitable"), and the targeted OpEx reduction.

Sentiment Analysis

  • Analysts: slightly negative to skeptical, highlighted by Jade Rahmani’s comment, "it seems challenging to raise $450 million of equity capital" and surprise at reduced emphasis on loan sales.
  • Management: slightly positive in prepared remarks and steady in Q&A, using confidence language such as "we're confident" and "we're highly confident" (Chairman, CEO & Chief Investment Officer Capasse), while CFO Ahlborn emphasized "a deceleration in the pressures" on results.
  • Versus last quarter, management messaging shifted from execution of large loan sales to stressing fewer sales and more financing/runoff, while analyst questioning remained focused on liquidity, leverage, and asset quality.

Quarter-over-Quarter Comparison

  • Q1 emphasized liquidity from loan sales: "we made the decision to delever the balance sheet with aggressive asset management focused primarily on loan sales" (Chairman, CEO & Chief Investment Officer Capasse, Q1). In Q2, management pivoted: "we do not anticipate further large portfolio sales" and "we are no longer budgeting loan sales" (Chairman, CEO & Chief Investment Officer Capasse, Q2).
  • The Ritz/Portland asset narrative evolved from progress metrics to monetization timing: Q2 added, "determine the optimal path forward ... whether that's continued stabilization or monetization" (Chairman, CEO & Chief Investment Officer Capasse).
  • SBA 7(a) shifted from pending capacity (Q1: "pending launch") to completed financing and a production target (Q2: "we expect steady growth towards our annual target of $1.5 billion of originations").

Risks and Concerns

  • "37% or roughly $1 billion of the loan book comprises sub and nonperforming assets" (Chairman, CEO & Chief Investment Officer Capasse), and he said the Ritz REO represents "approximately 22% of quarter end stockholders' equity."
  • Liquidity execution risk remains tied to specific actions: "optimizing the financing of approximately $950 million of CRE loans" and action on the "$118 million joint venture position" (Chairman, CEO & Chief Investment Officer Capasse).
  • Management’s mitigation centered on asset-level financing and operating cost reductions: "We are executing a targeted cost optimization program" (Chairman, CEO & Chief Investment Officer Capasse) and "we expect net interest income to continue improving as nonaccrual loans and REO are resolved" (CFO & Secretary Ahlborn).

Final Takeaway

Management characterized Q2 as progress in repositioning, stating it does not expect further large portfolio sales and instead plans to finish 2026 maturities through financing optimization, portfolio runoff, and potential monetization/financing of a joint venture LP interest. Leadership also tied a return to profitability to resolving legacy CRE/REO earnings drag, ramping SBA 7(a) toward a $1.5 billion annual origination target supported by ABS capacity, and implementing a targeted 25% to 35% operating expense reduction.
